nodes.label: entity<T>(req)
nodes.rationale: Reduces Content-Type to its bare media type, picks a serializer, decodes req.body and casts. Throws 400 on a missing or malformed body and 415 on a type nothing decodes. Matching is on the parsed media type, so naming a known type inside a parameter does not select that serializer.

nodes.label: marshal
nodes.rationale: Content-negotiated response encoding driven by the Accept header - CBOR for application/cbor, JSON otherwise. Worth it when different clients want different formats (IoT on CBOR, browsers on JSON) or bandwidth justifies CBOR; otherwise completeJson.

nodes.label: JsonSerializer
nodes.rationale: Standard JSON via JSON.stringify/parse with UTF-8 bytes; also the fallback when no Content-Type is sent at all.

nodes.label: CborSerializer
nodes.rationale: CBOR (RFC 8949): typically 20-40% smaller than JSON and first-class for binary fields with no base64 wrapping. JSON remains the better choice for human-debuggable APIs.

nodes.label: Serializer interface
nodes.rationale: A two-method contract (toBinary/fromBinary) that custom formats such as Protobuf or MessagePack can implement - but the HTTP module's media-type-to-serializer map is a private constant, so custom types must be branched on before calling entity.

nodes.label: 415 for unknown Content-Type
nodes.rationale: An undecodable Content-Type is a 415 rather than a speculative JSON parse, and the accepted list ships as an Accept response header per RFC 9110 12.5.1. Two deliberate exceptions: a missing Content-Type still decodes as JSON (RFC 9110 leaves the recipient free to guess, and HttpClient only sets the header for object bodies), and structured-syntax suffixes such as +json follow their base type per RFC 6839.

nodes.label: entity<T> does not validate
nodes.rationale: The cast is trust-based: TypeScript believes the type, the runtime value is unknown. The framework deliberately bundles no validator, so layer zod/valibot/io-ts on top of entity<unknown>.
